planting.note: Direct sow in fall to allow natural winter cold-moist stratification, or cold-stratify seed in the refrigerator for 4-6 weeks and sow in early spring. Southwestern red columbine germinates and establishes slowly, typically flowering in its second year.

directions: Grow in gravelly, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath conifers or on rocky slopes, echoing the montane forest habitat of this Four Corners-region native found from 6,500 to 10,000 feet in Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, and Utah. Aquilegia elegantula produces slender, nodding, red-and-yellow flowers with short, gently curved spurs that are noticeably more delicate than those of its lookalike relative Aquilegia formosa, and it blooms a few weeks later, extending the native columbine season into midsummer at higher elevations. Hummingbirds are the primary pollinators of the red-and-yellow flower form, and the plant self-sows modestly to form loose colonies without becoming aggressive. Give it consistent moisture through its first two seasons; established plants tolerate the drier, well-drained conditions typical of the Southern Rockies once their roots are deep.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold-moist stratification and spring emergence, or cold-stratify refrigerated seed 4 weeks before sowing in late winter. Keep seedbeds consistently moist, since this seep-dwelling species does not tolerate drying out the way most western columbines do.

directions: Plant in constantly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, recreating the seeps, streambanks, and serpentine-influenced slopes of the California Coast Ranges and southern Sierra Nevada foothills where this species grows wild. Unlike most western columbines, Aquilegia eximia thrives with wet roots through the growing season and is an excellent choice for the boggy edge of a pond or a spot below a downspout; its tall stems carry deep crimson-red, long-spurred flowers into summer, later than most other native columbines. Hummingbirds visit the flowers frequently, and the plant tolerates the heavy clay or mineral-rich soils associated with serpentine outcrops that few other garden perennials can handle. It is short-lived but reseeds reliably where moisture is dependable.

planting.note: Sow in fall into gritty, mineral scree mix and leave containers outdoors to receive winter cold and freeze-thaw cycles, which alpine columbine seed requires for reliable germination; some seed may not sprout until its second spring.

directions: Grow in a scree bed or trough with sharply drained, gritty, mineral-rich soil and full sun, mimicking the granite talus and rocky slopes of the high Sierra Nevada above 9,000 feet where this species is found. Aquilegia pubescens is among the showiest of the true alpine columbines, forming a tight mound of blue-green foliage topped by relatively large, upward-facing flowers in shades of cream, pale yellow, or dusty pink with short spurs. It resents winter wet far more than summer drought, so a top-dressing of grit around the crown and a raised, fast-draining site are essential for longevity outside its native range. Established plants are long-lived where the drainage is right but will rot quickly in heavy or poorly drained garden soil.

planting.note: Sow in fall in a gritty scree mix and expose to natural winter freezing, since seed of this high-elevation species germinates best after several weeks of cold; keep the medium barely moist over winter to avoid rot.

directions: Site in a raised scree bed, crevice garden, or trough with fast-draining, gritty, alkaline soil and full sun, replicating the limestone and sandstone cliffs and talus of the Colorado Plateau and Uinta and Wasatch ranges where Aquilegia scopulorum grows. This dwarf alpine forms a low cushion of finely divided, blue-gray foliage and carries pale lavender-blue to whitish flowers with short, curved spurs just above the leaves in early summer. It is intolerant of summer humidity and wet, heavy soils, and gardeners outside dry mountain climates generally need a covered scree bed or alpine house to keep it happy long-term. Water sparingly through summer dormancy once established.

planting.note: Sow immediately after collection or purchase into a mineral scree mix and leave outdoors through winter, since fresh seed and prolonged natural cold are both important for germination; older seed germinates erratically if at all. Seedlings grow very slowly and may take several years to reach flowering size.

directions: Reserve this true miniature alpine for a tufa rock, crevice garden, or alpine house, planted in pure mineral grit with minimal organic matter, in full sun with cool nights, to imitate the limestone scree of its native Wyoming and Montana Rocky Mountain ranges above treeline. Aquilegia jonesii forms a tiny, tight cushion of silvery, finely divided leaves barely an inch or two tall, studded in early summer with disproportionately large blue-violet flowers held just above the foliage. It is famously one of the most difficult alpine plants to keep alive outside its native scree, demanding bone-dry dormancy in winter and never being allowed to sit in wet soil at any time of year. Most gardeners who succeed with it use a raised, covered scree bed or grow it in a pot plunged in grit under glass.

common_name: Limestone Columbine (Colorado Plateau Hanging Garden Columbine)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall to allow winter cold-moist stratification, or cold-stratify seed for 3-4 weeks before sowing in spring. Keep the seedbed reliably moist, since this species naturally roots in perpetually damp sandstone seeps rather than typical garden soil.

directions: Plant in a consistently damp, sandy or gravelly, well-drained pocket in partial to full shade, echoing the sandstone alcove seeps and 'hanging gardens' of the Colorado Plateau in Utah, Colorado, and Arizona where Aquilegia micrantha clings to vertical cliff faces. It bears small, pale blue to nearly white nodding flowers with short spurs on slender stems, more delicate and diminutive than most other native columbines, and blooms over a long season where moisture is dependable. In cultivation it does best at the moist edge of a rock garden, a container with a constantly wet saucer, or near a garden seep, since it will not persist in soil that dries out between waterings. It self-sows into damp crevices when conditions suit it, forming small colonies over time.

common_name: Origami Columbine (Compact Colorado Blue Columbine Strain)

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost after 3-4 weeks of cold-moist stratification; sown early enough, 'Origami' reliably blooms its first summer, unlike the straight species, which typically takes two years to flower.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, or morning sun with afternoon shade in warmer zones, the same conditions favored by its parent species, the Colorado state flower Aquilegia caerulea. 'Origami' was bred as a compact, uniform seed strain that keeps the species' large, long-spurred, blue-and-white bicolor blooms while reducing overall height to about a foot, making it far more useful for borders, containers, and small gardens than the taller wild form. Its main advantage over open-pollinated straight Aquilegia caerulea is speed to bloom: started early indoors, it flowers the same year it is sown rather than waiting until its second season. Deadhead to tidy the plant, or allow some seed to mature and self-sow, though seedlings from 'Origami' will not always come true to the compact habit.
